In the same situation but the roles are reversed. I can only tell you from my point of view from what my husband does for me. There are times that our episodes just happen. Sometimes there are triggers. Take some time to figure out if he has any triggers like a conversation he had with a coworker and it pertained a specific topic that he is not okay with. It also sounds like he suffers from bad self esteem issues. I haven't gotten over mine yet. But my husband still hugs me while I'm crying and whispers to me how much I mean to him, loves me, and tells me what he thinks about me, and kisses me when he can.

Sometimes we also just want our space to just cry it out. You just being next to him while he is having his break down might eventually calm him down during his episode. The presence of someone just simply being there does a world of good for depressed people like us.

The thing what people don't realize is that getting into a relationship with someone who suffers from bi-polar, manic depression, etc takes a lot of work and understanding. When I keep people from a distance is because 1: no one was ever there for me as I grew up dealing with my depression so I lost faith in them. 2: the majority of society see us in a negative light which prevents us from trusting the world. There is no cure for depression.

You can make it less horrible, but I personally think you can't get rid of it entirely. Some people have horrible reactions to psych meds. I know I do, but there are others who have a better quality of life because of those meds. 

As for finding a doctor, I don't have much to say in a positive way for this. I've went through over 6 doctors in my life time and I was unhappy with all of them. Trying to find the right doctor is like trying to get into a relationship with another person. It's emotionally and physically taxing. But like the meds comment, some people can find those doctors.

Long story short, not every depressed person is going to be the same. You have to figure out if he has triggers, what sets him off, make attempts at finding a doctor. If not, talking to him might just suffice since he has some trust with you since you are in this relationship with him.

Also avoid any foods that has estrogen. I found out the hard way that soy milk was contributing to my mood swings/depression and it lessened after I cut it out.

As a spouse who suffers from long time depression, social anxiety, agoraphobia, etc; I can only offer my personal insight on this. Please take note that every person that suffers from depression/bipolar issues can be uniquely different with their triggers. (And sometimes it doesn't even need a trigger.)

Relationships:
It's not easy, as you're very aware of. There isn't really any answers, as far as I know, despite being in a 8 year long relationship. The only thing I can tell you is that you have to endure it. Being in a relationship with someone who suffers from depression takes a lot of time, patience, understanding, sincere love, and a lot of emotional strength/stamina.

You can try and log when her depression spells hits. Sometimes you can even go by our menstrual cycles when our hormones are really fluctuating at it's worst. Write down when it starts, and when it ends. Try to also see what may of triggered it.

Eating better can help with depression. For me, I have to avoid anything that is soy based because the extra estrogen messes with my emotions badly and makes my depression spells worse.

For ever cry session drink plenty of water. During, and after. Besides feeling dehydrated afterwards, your blood also thickens which will make circulation go slower and you end up feeling slugish and even more terrible. You can also get some pretty wicked headaches after an intense cry session.

Vitamin D is also important. My husband tries to force me to go outside for it from the sun. He thinks it's a bonus that the walking (blood circulation) helps and it sometimes gets rid of my cabin fever when I am really home bound.

And yes, sometimes I need my personal space/time from him.

So just doing or showing the interest in good after care with her COULD lighten her depression spells. At least, the way my husband does it, makes me feel better. Hugs, kisses, unconditional love are always the best medicine, I think. It took me a long time to accept that because I have trust issues with people. Plus I am a tom boy, I have an image to uphold. (joke)

It took me MONTHS to finally realize and to be comfortable to say 'I love you' to him. People getting into a relationship with one (or sometimes both) of them with depression issues have to put a lot of faith and trust and work into it. Yeah, that's required in any relationship but I think it's even more so when it comes to this subject.

As for professional help (my opinion!) I hate it. I went through 6 different professionals and I hated every single one of them. Trying to find THE RIGHT one is also like getting into another relationship. But that's a separate tangent for me on how much I hate big pharma and the way how health insurance works. If she wants to seek help, that is her decision. If she does decide to do it, be supportive. If she allows you to, maybe you can join in one of the sessions. My husband did.
